lead: A loop much smaller than a wavelength carries nearly the same current all the way round, so it behaves as a magnetic dipole: the short dipole’s doughnut pattern with E and H exchanged. Its radiation resistance grows as the fourth power of its size, so it radiates poorly; as a receiver that hardly matters, which is why a coil on a ferrite rod sits in every AM radio.
prereq: You need: the Hertzian dipole field and radiation efficiency.

blocks.text: A loop antenna is a conductor bent into a closed shape (circle or square) with a feed gap. For a circle of radius a the circumference is C = 2πa. The loop is small when C ≤ λ/10. The phase then changes by at most 36° round the loop, so the current is one value I everywhere.
A uniform current loop is a magnetic dipole with moment
m = N I A. m in A·m²; N is the number of turns; I the current in A; A the area of one turn in m² (πa² for a circle). m points along the loop axis by the right-hand rule

The loop is the twin of the short electric dipole: both have the sin θ pattern and D = 1.5, but the loop radiates E<sub>φ</sub> and H<sub>θ</sub> where the dipole radiates E<sub>θ</sub> and H<sub>φ</sub>.
Eφ = 120π² N I A sin θ / (λ² r). Eφ in V/m; θ is measured from the loop axis; r in m; Hθ = −Eφ/η
The pattern is largest in the plane of the loop and zero along its axis; E lies in the loop’s plane. Integrating |E<sub>φ</sub>|²/(2η) over a sphere and setting it equal to ½ I² R<sub>r</sub> gives
Rr = 320π⁴ (N A / λ²)² ≈ 31 171 (N A / λ²)² Ω. A in m², λ in m

For a single circular turn A = C²/4π, which turns this into Rr = 20π² (C/λ)⁴. The fourth power is the whole story. A single turn of 1 m² at λ = 30 m (10 MHz) has Rr = 31 171 × (1/900)² = 0.038 Ω. Halve its radius and the area falls four times while Rr falls sixteen times. Rr grows as N² while loss grows roughly as N, so turns help only slowly.
Its input impedance is a small resistance plus a large inductive reactance, tuned out by a capacitor; the high Q makes a small loop narrow-band.

Medium-wave broadcasting runs from about 530 kHz to 1.6 MHz, where λ is 566 m to 188 m. A loop with C = λ/10 would be 6 m to 18 m across, so a coil is wound on a ferrite rod instead. The rod gathers flux, so the coil acts as if its area were μ<sub>eff</sub> A; the effective permeability μ<sub>eff</sub> of a short rod is well below the ferrite’s μ<sub>r</sub> but still tens to a few hundred.

On receive, the induced voltage is V = E leff with an effective length leff = 2π N μeff A / λ, so the rod raises the received voltage by μeff and the radiation resistance by μeff². The rod’s null lies along its axis, which is why a portable radio is turned until the rod lies broadside to the station.

A loop null is a true zero with the pattern rising as sin θ ≈ θ beside it, so turning a loop for the null gives a bearing to a degree or two. The two nulls are 180° apart; adding a short vertical sense antenna gives a heart-shaped pattern with one null and removes the doubt.

figure.caption: A small loop is a magnetic dipole: its moment m = NIA points along the axis, where the field is zero, and it radiates most in its own plane. For the worked example’s 10-turn loop at 10 MHz, R<sub>r</sub> is only 3.8 mΩ against 0.05 Ω of loss, so 7 per cent of the power radiates.

spec.aria: A loop seen edge-on with its axis vertical and the moment m = N I A drawn along the axis. Two pattern lobes extend left and right, in the plane of the loop, with nulls along the axis. A panel gives the worked example: 10 turns of radius 0.1 metre at 10 megahertz, radiation resistance 3.8 milliohm, loss 0.05 ohm, efficiency 7 percent.

examples.question: A small loop has N = 10 turns of radius a = 0.1 m and works at 10 MHz. Its loss resistance is 0.05 Ω. Check that it is small, and find its radiation resistance and radiation efficiency.
steps: C = 2π × 0.1 = 0.628 m and λ/10 = 3 m, so C < λ/10: the loop is small.
η<sub>rad</sub> = R<sub>r</sub>/(R<sub>r</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>) = 0.0038/0.0538 = 0.071, about 7 per cent.
examples.answer: The loop is small (0.628 m < 3 m); R<sub>r</sub> = 3.8 mΩ; η<sub>rad</sub> ≈ 7 per cent.

examples.question: An AM radio has a 60-turn coil on a ferrite rod 10 mm in diameter with μ<sub>eff</sub> = 80, tuned to 1 MHz. The station gives a field of 1 mV/m at the radio. Find the effective length of the rod antenna and the open-circuit voltage induced in the coil, and its radiation resistance.
steps: λ = 3 × 10⁸ / 10⁶ = 300 m. Area of one turn: A = π × 0.005² = 7.854 × 10⁻⁵ m².
l<sub>eff</sub> = 2π N μ<sub>eff</sub> A/λ = 2π × 60 × 80 × 7.854 × 10⁻⁵ / 300 = 7.90 × 10⁻³ m, about 8 mm.
V<sub>oc</sub> = E l<sub>eff</sub> = 10⁻³ × 7.90 × 10⁻³ = 7.9 × 10⁻⁶ V = 7.9 µV (rod broadside to the station).
The coil’s own resistance is ohms, so η<sub>rad</sub> is around 10⁻⁷: hopeless as a transmitter, yet the 7.9 µV, raised by the Q of the tuned circuit, is plenty for the receiver.
examples.answer: l<sub>eff</sub> ≈ 7.9 mm; V<sub>oc</sub> ≈ 7.9 µV; R<sub>r</sub> ≈ 5.5 × 10⁻⁷ Ω.

traps: Dropping N from R<sub>r</sub> = 31 171 (NA/λ²)². The turns are inside the bracket and are squared with the area.
Using the diameter as the radius in A = πa². The area comes out four times too large and R<sub>r</sub> sixteen times too large; using the wire radius makes it far too small.
Mixing up the nulls. A short dipole has its null along the wire; a small loop has its null along its axis, perpendicular to the plane of the loop.
Using the small-loop formulas when C is not below λ/10. The current is then not uniform and the pattern and R<sub>r</sub> change.
Entering the area in cm² or λ in cm. The constant 31 171 assumes metres.

quiz.q: State the condition for a loop to be treated as small and what it guarantees.
quiz.a: C ≤ λ/10. The current is then nearly the same in amplitude and phase all round the loop.

quiz.q: Write the magnetic moment of an N-turn loop with its unit and direction.
quiz.a: m = NIA in A·m², along the loop axis by the right-hand rule with the fingers along the current.

quiz.q: Why is a small loop called a magnetic dipole, and how do its far fields differ from a short electric dipole’s?
quiz.a: Its far field is that of a magnetic moment m = NIA. It radiates E<sub>φ</sub> and H<sub>θ</sub>, where the dipole radiates E<sub>θ</sub> and H<sub>φ</sub>; the sin θ pattern and D = 1.5 are the same.

quiz.q: A single circular turn of radius 0.5 m works at 10 MHz. Find R<sub>r</sub> and say whether the formula is valid.
quiz.a: λ = 30 m, C = 3.14 m, just over λ/10 = 3 m, so the result is only approximate. A = 0.785 m², A/λ² = 8.73 × 10⁻⁴, R<sub>r</sub> = 31 171 × 7.62 × 10⁻⁷ = 0.024 Ω.

quiz.q: A 20-turn loop of radius 0.05 m works at 30 MHz with R<sub>L</sub> = 0.1 Ω. Find R<sub>r</sub> and η<sub>rad</sub>.
Explain why R<sub>r</sub> of a small loop goes as the fourth power of its size, and what that means for a medium-wave receiving antenna.
quiz.a: The far field is proportional to m = NIA, so power and R<sub>r</sub> go as A², and A goes as the square of the radius. At medium wave λ is hundreds of metres, so an air loop of hand size has R<sub>r</sub> far below its loss; a ferrite rod multiplies the effective area by μ<sub>eff</sub> and the voltage with it, and the receiver needs voltage, not efficiency.

quiz.q: Why is a loop null good for direction finding, and how is the 180° doubt removed?
quiz.a: The null is a true zero and the pattern rises as sin θ ≈ θ beside it, so a one-degree turn changes the signal sharply. The two nulls are 180° apart; adding a sense antenna gives a heart-shaped pattern with a single null.

beyond: Not for the exam. NFC cards, RFID tags and wireless chargers use small loops in the reactive near field, as coupled coils rather than radiators. Large loops (C about λ) radiate most along their axis and lead to quad and helical antennas. Search next for “Adcock direction finder” and “Chu limit”.
